name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Evolution of fumes from halide salts

questiontext.text: On addition of conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to a chloride salt, colourless fumes are evolved but in case of iodide salt, violet fumes come out. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) acts as both a strong acid and a moderately strong oxidising agent. When reacting with halide salts, the nature of the evolved gas depends directly on the ease of oxidation (reducing strength) of the resulting hydrogen halide.

Step 2: Reaction with Chloride Salts
When concentrated sulphuric acid is added to a chloride salt such as sodium chloride, hydrogen chloride gas is produced:
\[\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO}_4 + \mathrm{HCl}\]
Because hydrogen chloride is a very weak reducing agent, sulphuric acid cannot oxidise it to chlorine gas. Consequently, colourless, pungent fumes of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) are evolved.

Step 3: Reaction with Iodide Salts
When concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with an iodide salt, hydrogen iodide is initially generated:
\[\mathrm{NaI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHSO}_4 + \mathrm{HI}\]
Hydrogen iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than hydrogen chloride due to the low bond dissociation enthalpy of the \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{I}\) bond. Concentrated sulphuric acid readily oxidises the formed \(\mathrm{HI}\) to elemental iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)) while being reduced itself to sulphur dioxide:
\[2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Elemental iodine vaporises to produce characteristic violet fumes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the violet fumes appear because \(\mathrm{HI}\) gets oxidised to \(\mathrm{I}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Deep blue solution of tetraamminecopper complex

questiontext.text: In qualitative analysis when \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) is passed through an aqueous solution of salt acidified with dil. \(\mathrm{HCl}\), a black precipitate is obtained. On boiling the precipitate with dil. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), it forms a solution of blue colour. Addition of excess of aqueous solution of ammonia to this solution gives

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In qualitative analysis, Group II cations precipitate as insoluble sulphides in acidic medium. Copper(II) cations form a black sulphide precipitate that dissolves in dilute nitric acid to generate hydrated cupric ions, which subsequently form a soluble ammine complex in excess ammonia.

Step 2: Precipitation and Dissolution Reactions
Passing \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) into the acidified cupric solution precipitates black copper(II) sulphide:
\[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuS}\downarrow + 2\mathrm{H}^+\]
Boiling this black precipitate with dilute nitric acid oxidises sulphide to elemental sulphur, dissolving the precipitate to form copper(II) nitrate and imparting a characteristic blue colour to the solution:
\[3\mathrm{CuS} + 8\mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 3\mathrm{S}\downarrow + 2\mathrm{NO}\uparrow + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Complex Formation with Excess Ammonia
Addition of excess aqueous ammonia results in the formation of the soluble tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion:
\[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{NH}_3 \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_4\right]^{2+}\]
This complex ion imparts an intense, deep blue colour to the solution.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the addition of excess aqueous ammonia gives a deep blue solution of \(\left[\mathrm{Cu}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4}\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Single and double bonds in cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid

questiontext.text: In a cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid molecule, how many single and double bonds are present?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The molecule under examination is cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid, \((\mathrm{HPO}_3)_3\), also represented as \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{P}_3\mathrm{O}_9\). It has a cyclic, six-membered alternating ring of phosphorus and oxygen atoms: \(-\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}-\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Structural Model
Each of the three phosphorus atoms in the ring is in the \(+5\) oxidation state and adopts tetrahedral coordination:
1. Two single bonds linking it to bridging oxygen atoms within the ring (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}\)).
2. One double bond linking it to a terminal oxygen atom (\(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O}\)).
3. One single bond linking it to a terminal hydroxyl group (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\)).
4. Each hydroxyl group contains an oxygen-hydrogen single bond (\(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The total numbers of bonds in the molecule are obtained by summing across the ring and the exocyclic groups:
- Number of double bonds = \(\sum (\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O})\)
- Number of single bonds = \(\sum (\text{ring } \mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}) + \sum (\text{terminal } \mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}) + \sum (\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H})\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Double bonds: Each phosphorus has 1 \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O}\) bond. For 3 phosphorus atoms, there are \(3 \times 1 = 3\) double bonds.
- Single bonds:
- The six-membered ring contains 3 bridging oxygen atoms, each contributing 2 \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}\) single bonds, giving \(3 \times 2 = 6\) ring single bonds.
- Each phosphorus is bonded to one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group via a \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{O}\) single bond, giving \(3 \times 1 = 3\) single bonds.
- Each of the three \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups contains an \(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) single bond, giving \(3 \times 1 = 3\) single bonds.
- Total single bonds = \(6 + 3 + 3 = 12\) single bonds.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The molecule contains 3 double bonds and 12 single bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Elements capable of forming d pi bonds

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements can be involved in \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) bonding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Formation of a \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) bond requires the sideways overlap between a \(\mathrm{p}\)-orbital of one atom and a vacant, accessible \(\mathrm{d}\)-orbital of another atom. Hence, only elements that possess vacant \(\mathrm{d}\)-orbitals in their valence shell can engage in \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) bonding.

Step 2: Electronic Configuration Analysis
- Boron (atomic number 5): \(1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^1\)
- Carbon (atomic number 6): \(1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^2\)
- Nitrogen (atomic number 7): \(1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^3\)
Boron, carbon, and nitrogen are second-period elements whose valence shell is \(n = 2\). Because the second principal energy level contains only \(2s\) and \(2p\) subshells, they lack \(\mathrm{d}\)-orbitals entirely and cannot participate in \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) bonding.
- Phosphorus (atomic number 15): \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2\, 3p^3\, 3d^0\)
Phosphorus belongs to the third period (\(n = 3\)) and has vacant, energetically accessible \(3d\)-orbitals in its valence shell.

Step 3: Application to Multiple Bonding
Using these vacant \(3d\)-orbitals, phosphorus can expand its octet and form \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) multiple bonds by overlapping with filled or half-filled \(2p\)-orbitals of elements like oxygen and nitrogen (as observed in oxoacids and phosphine oxides).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, phosphorus is the element that can be involved in \(\mathrm{p\pi}\text{–}\mathrm{d\pi}\) bonding.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Isoelectronic and isostructural pair of polyatomic ions

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of ions are isoelectronic and isostructural?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemical species are isoelectronic if they have identical total numbers of electrons. They are isostructural if their central atoms exhibit the same hybridisation state and the same spatial arrangement of constituent atoms.

Step 2: Electron Count Evaluation
- For carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\)):
Total electrons = \(6\,(\text{C}) + 3 \times 8\,(\text{O}) + 2 = 32\) electrons.
- For nitrate ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\)):
Total electrons = \(7\,(\text{N}) + 3 \times 8\,(\text{O}) + 1 = 32\) electrons.
Both \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) possess 32 electrons and are therefore isoelectronic.

Step 3: Geometry and Hybridisation Analysis
- In \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\), the central carbon atom forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds and has zero lone pairs. Steric number is 3, corresponding to \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridisation and a trigonal planar geometry.
- In \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\), the central nitrogen atom forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds and has zero lone pairs. Steric number is 3, corresponding to \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridisation and a trigonal planar geometry.
Since both ions adopt a trigonal planar geometry, they are isostructural.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the pair of ions that are both isoelectronic and isostructural is \(\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-},\, \mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Highest bond dissociation enthalpy among halogen acids

questiontext.text: Affinity for hydrogen decreases in the group from fluorine to iodine. Which of the halogen acids should have highest bond dissociation enthalpy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond dissociation enthalpy is determined primarily by the bond length and the degree of orbital overlap between the bonded atoms. Smaller atomic radii allow closer approach and more effective overlap, yielding stronger bonds and higher dissociation enthalpies.

Step 2: Periodic Trend in Halogen Size
Moving down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine, atomic radius increases: \(\mathrm{F} < \mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{I}\). Consequently, the bond length of hydrogen halides increases in the order:
\[\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{F} < \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{I}\]

Step 3: Comparison of Bond Strengths
Fluorine has the smallest atomic radius and the highest electronegativity, resulting in strong orbital overlap between the \(1s\) orbital of hydrogen and the \(2p\) orbital of fluorine. Because bond strength decreases with increasing bond length, the bond dissociation enthalpy decreases down the group:
\[\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{F} > \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Br} > \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{I}\]
Among all halogen acids, \(\mathrm{HF}\) has the highest bond dissociation enthalpy (approximately \(567\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\mathrm{HF}\) has the highest bond dissociation enthalpy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Strongest reducing agent among group fifteen hydrides

questiontext.text:
Bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{E—H}\) (\(\mathrm{E} = \text{element}\)) bonds is given below. Which of the compounds will act as strongest reducing agent?

Compound\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)\(\mathrm{AsH}_3\)\(\mathrm{SbH}_3\)
\(\Delta_{\text{diss}} (\mathrm{E—H})/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)389322297255

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The bond dissociation enthalpies (\(\Delta_{\text{diss}}(\mathrm{E—H})\)) are:
- \(\mathrm{NH}_3\): \(389\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
- \(\mathrm{PH}_3\): \(322\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
- \(\mathrm{AsH}_3\): \(297\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
- \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\): \(255\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical Principles
The reducing power of a covalent hydride is governed by its ability to release hydrogen. A weaker \(\mathrm{E—H}\) bond dissociates more readily, facilitating hydrogen liberation and resulting in stronger reducing capability.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reducing power is inversely related to bond dissociation enthalpy:
\[\text{Reducing power} \propto \frac{1}{\Delta_{\text{diss}}(\mathrm{E—H})}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the given values:
\[255\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} (\mathrm{SbH}_3) < 297\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} (\mathrm{AsH}_3) < 322\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} (\mathrm{PH}_3) < 389\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} (\mathrm{NH}_3)\]
Since \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) has the lowest bond dissociation enthalpy (\(255\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)), the \(\mathrm{Sb}-\mathrm{H}\) bond is the weakest and cleaves most easily.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) is the strongest reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Characteristics of phosphine gas from white phosphorus

questiontext.text: On heating with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), white phosphorus gives a gas. Which of the following statement is incorrect about the gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle and Reaction
When white phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}_4\)) is heated with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), it undergoes disproportionation to form phosphine gas (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)) and sodium hypophosphite:
\[\mathrm{P}_4 + 3\mathrm{NaOH} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{PH}_3\uparrow + 3\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\]
Thus, the gas produced is phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Gas Properties
- Phosphine is extremely poisonous and possesses an unpleasant odour like rotten fish.
- In water and in the presence of light, phosphine decomposes slowly into red phosphorus and dihydrogen gas.
- Basicity comparison: In ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)), the nitrogen atom is small and its lone pair resides in an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybrid orbital with high directional electron density. In phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)), the phosphorus atom is larger and the lone pair resides predominantly in an unhybridised, diffuse \(3s\) orbital. Consequently, the lone pair on phosphorus is much less available for donation to a proton, making phosphine significantly less basic than ammonia.

Step 3: Identification of the Incorrect Statement
Because phosphine is a much weaker base than ammonia, the assertion stating that the gas is more basic than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is false.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the incorrect statement about the gas is that it is more basic than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\).

answer.text: It is highly poisonous and has smell like rotten fish.
It's solution in water decomposes in the presence of light.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Acid capable of forming three series of salts

questiontext.text: Which of the following acids forms three series of salts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An oxoacid forms as many series of salts as its basicity. The basicity of an oxoacid of phosphorus is determined by the number of ionisable protons, which correspond solely to hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen as hydroxyl groups (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)). Hydrogen atoms bonded directly to phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\)) do not dissociate as protons in aqueous solution.

Step 2: Analysis of the Given Acids
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) (hypophosphorous acid): Contains one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds. It is monobasic and forms only one series of salts.
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\) (boric acid): Acts as a weak, monobasic Lewis acid in water by accepting \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) from water, forming only one series of salts.
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) (orthophosphorous acid): Contains two \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and one \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bond. It is dibasic and forms two series of salts.
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) (orthophosphoric acid): Contains three \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups attached to the central phosphorus atom. It is tribasic and dissociates in three successive stages.

Step 3: Salt Series Formation
Because \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) is tribasic, it forms three distinct series of salts: dihydrogen phosphates (such as \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_4\)), monohydrogen phosphates (such as \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{HPO}_4\)), and normal phosphates (such as \(\mathrm{Na}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the acid that forms three series of salts is \(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{PO}_{4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Structural origin of reducing behaviour of hypophosphorous acid

questiontext.text: Strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{PO}_{2}\) is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reducing properties of phosphorus oxoacids arise from the presence of hydrogen atoms directly attached to the phosphorus atom (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds). These hydrogen atoms possess hydridic character and can readily be oxidised, enabling the acid to act as an effective reducing agent.

Step 2: Molecular Structure of Hypophosphorous Acid
In hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\), also known as phosphinic acid), the central phosphorus atom is tetrahedrally bonded to:
- One double-bonded oxygen atom (\(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{O}\)).
- One single-bonded hydroxyl group (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{OH}\)).
- Two hydrogen atoms directly attached to phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\)).

Step 3: Relationship Between Structure and Reducing Property
The presence of two \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds gives \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) strong reducing behaviour, such as its ability to reduce silver nitrate to metallic silver. The single \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group imparts monobasic character to the acid.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{PO}_{2}\) is due to the presence of one -OH group and two P-H bonds.

answer.text: Presence of two -OH groups and one P-H bond
Presence of one -OH group and two P-H bonds

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Thermal decomposition products of lead nitrate salt

questiontext.text: On heating lead nitrate forms oxides of nitrogen and lead. The oxides formed are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nitrates of heavy metals decompose upon thermal heating to yield the corresponding metal monoxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and dioxygen gas.

Step 2: Chemical Decomposition Reaction
When solid lead(II) nitrate is strongly heated, it undergoes decomposition according to the equation:
\[2\mathrm{Pb(NO}_3)_2 \\xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{PbO} + 4\mathrm{NO}_2\uparrow + \mathrm{O}_2\uparrow\]

Step 3: Identification of Product Oxides
The reaction produces lead(II) oxide (\(\mathrm{PbO}\), a yellow solid residue) and nitrogen dioxide (\(\mathrm{NO}_2\), a reddish-brown, pungent gas). Oxygen is also evolved as elemental gas.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the oxides of nitrogen and lead formed on heating lead nitrate are \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Absence of allotropy in nitrogen family elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements does not show allotropy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Allotropy refers to the existence of a chemical element in two or more distinct physical forms having different structural arrangements and bonding networks in the same physical state.

Step 2: Allotropy in Group 15 Elements
Elements of Group 15 such as phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony readily form various allotropes (such as white, red, and black phosphorus; yellow and grey arsenic; yellow and metallic antimony) because they can form stable single covalent bonds that assemble into catenated chains, rings, or layered sheets. Bismuth also exhibits crystalline allotropic forms.

Step 3: Unique Nature of Nitrogen
Nitrogen is exceptionally small in atomic size, which causes severe interelectronic repulsion between the non-bonding electron lone pairs of adjacent nitrogen atoms in a single bond. As a result, the single \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{N}\) bond is very weak compared to the extraordinarily stable triple bond (\(\mathrm{N}\equiv\mathrm{N}\)) found in the diatomic molecule. Because nitrogen cannot form stable catenated polymeric networks, it exists solely as discrete \(\mathrm{N}_2\) molecules and does not show allotropy.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, nitrogen does not show allotropy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Valence shell orbital limitations on nitrogen covalency

questiontext.text: Maximum covalency of nitrogen is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The covalency of an element is the maximum number of shared electron-pair bonds that its atom can form. It is strictly limited by the total number of valence orbitals available for bonding in its outer shell.

Step 2: Electronic Configuration Analysis
The atomic number of nitrogen is 7, with valence shell electron configuration \(2s^2\, 2p_x^1\, 2p_y^1\, 2p_z^1\). The valence shell has principal quantum number \(n = 2\), which contains only one \(2s\) orbital and three \(2p\) orbitals, providing a total of four orbitals.

Step 3: Evaluation of Covalency Expansion
Because there are no \(\mathrm{d}\)-orbitals in the second shell, nitrogen cannot expand its valence shell beyond an octet. It can use at most four orbitals (one \(2s\) and three \(2p\)) to form bonds (for example, four covalent/coordinate bonds in \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) or \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\)). Thus, its maximum covalency is 4.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the maximum covalency of nitrogen is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Evaluation of bonding and properties of nitrogen compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is wrong?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle and Single Bond Comparison
Due to the very small atomic radius of nitrogen, non-bonding electron lone pairs on neighbouring nitrogen atoms are held closely together, resulting in high interelectronic repulsion. This makes the single \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{N}\) bond weak (bond enthalpy \(\approx 160\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). In contrast, the larger size of phosphorus reduces lone pair repulsions, resulting in a significantly stronger single \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{P}\) bond (bond enthalpy \(\approx 201\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)). Thus, the statement asserting that the single \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{N}\) bond is stronger than the single \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{P}\) bond is incorrect.

Step 2: Verification of Other Statements
- Phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)) has a lone pair of electrons on the phosphorus atom and acts as a Lewis base ligand, coordinating with transition metals.
- Nitrogen dioxide (\(\mathrm{NO}_2\)) is an odd-electron molecule containing 23 electrons in total (17 valence electrons) with an unpaired electron, making it paramagnetic in nature.
- In \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\), each nitrogen atom forms four covalent bonds (two single bonds, one double bond, or equivalent resonance structures involving a coordinate bond), resulting in a covalency of four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the statement that is wrong is that the single N-N bond is stronger than the single P-P bond.

answer.text: Single N-N bond is stronger than the single P-P bond.
\(\mathrm{PH}_3\) can act as a ligand in the formation of coordination compound with transition elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Coordination complex responsible for brown ring test

questiontext.text: A brown ring is formed in the ring test for \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) ion. It is due to the formation of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The brown ring test is a qualitative analytical test used to detect nitrate ions. It depends on the reduction of nitrate to nitric oxide by iron(II) ions in an acidic medium, followed by the coordination of nitric oxide to iron(II) to form a coloured complex.

Step 2: Chemical Reactions Involved
1. Nitrate ion is reduced by ferrous ion in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form nitric oxide:
\[\mathrm{NO}_3^- + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{NO} + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
2. The generated nitric oxide combines with the hexaaquairon(II) complex to form the brown coordination entity:
\[\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_6\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{NO} \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_5(\mathrm{NO})\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Identity of the Brown Ring
The distinctive brown ring that appears at the junction of the acid and aqueous layers is composed of the pentaaquanitrosyliron(II) complex, \(\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\right)_{5}(\mathrm{NO})\right]^{2+}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the brown ring is formed due to \(\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\right)_{5}(\mathrm{NO})\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Characterised pentavalent compound formed by bismuth

questiontext.text: Elements of group-15 form compounds in +5 oxidation state. However, bismuth forms only one well characterised compound in +5 oxidation state. The compound is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Descending Group 15, the stability of the \(+5\) oxidation state decreases while that of the \(+3\) oxidation state increases. This trend is caused by the inert pair effect, which arises from the poor shielding of the nucleus by intervening \(4f\) and \(5d\) electrons, making the valence \(6s^2\) electron pair less available for bond formation.

Step 2: Requirements to Stabilise High Oxidation States
To oxidise bismuth to its pentavalent state, the ligand must possess very small size, exceptionally high electronegativity, and high oxidising power to provide sufficient bond energy to overcome the promotional and ionisation energy demands.

Step 3: Characterised Pentavalent Compound
Fluorine meets these criteria because of its small atomic radius and high electronegativity. Hence, bismuth pentafluoride (\(\mathrm{BiF}_5\)) is the only stable, well-characterised compound in which bismuth exhibits the \(+5\) oxidation state. Other bismuth pentahalides like \(\mathrm{BiCl}_5\) do not exist because chloride is readily oxidised by \(\mathrm{Bi}(\mathrm{V})\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the only well-characterised compound of bismuth in the +5 oxidation state is \(\mathrm{BiF}_5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate and barium azide

questiontext.text: On heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately we get

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain nitrogen salts decompose on heating to release dinitrogen gas (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)). Thermal decomposition reactions can proceed either via intramolecular redox reactions or through pure thermal cleavage of azides.

Step 2: Decomposition of Ammonium Dichromate
Ammonium dichromate, \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7\), undergoes thermal decomposition in an intramolecular redox process to yield dinitrogen gas, green chromium(III) oxide, and water vapour:
\[(\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{N}_2\uparrow + \mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Decomposition of Barium Azide
Barium azide, \(\mathrm{Ba(N_3)_2}\), decomposes cleanly upon heating to produce pure dinitrogen gas and metallic barium:
\[\mathrm{Ba(N}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Ba} + 3\mathrm{N}_2\uparrow\]
This reaction is widely employed in laboratories to obtain ultra-pure dinitrogen.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately produces \(\mathrm{N}_2\) in both cases.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{N}_2\) with ammonium dichromate and NO with barium azide
\(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) with ammonium dichromate and \(\mathrm{N}_2\) with barium azide
\(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) with ammonium dichromate and \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) with barium azide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Stoichiometric yield of nitric oxide from ammonia oxidation

questiontext.text: In the preparation of \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), we get NO gas by catalytic oxidation of ammonia. The moles of NO produced by the oxidation of two moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Chemical process: Catalytic oxidation of ammonia to nitric oxide in Ostwald's process.
- Amount of reactant: \(n(\mathrm{NH}_3) = 2\,\text{moles}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Chemical Principles
The catalytic oxidation of ammonia occurs using excess atmospheric oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst gauze at \(500\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(9\,\mathrm{bar}\), proceeding according to standard reaction stoichiometry.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The balanced chemical equation for the catalytic oxidation of ammonia is:
\[4\mathrm{NH}_3 + 5\mathrm{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pt/Rh}} 4\mathrm{NO} + 6\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the balanced reaction equation:
4 moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) react to produce 4 moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\).
The stoichiometric mole ratio is:
\[\frac{n(\mathrm{NO})}{n(\mathrm{NH}_3)} = \frac{4}{4} = 1\]
Therefore, when 2 moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) undergo catalytic oxidation:
\[n(\mathrm{NO}) = 1 \times 2 = 2\,\text{moles}\]<\/p>

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The number of moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) produced is 2.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Oxidation state of phosphorus in sodium hypophosphite

questiontext.text: The oxidation state of central atom in the anion of compound \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- Compound: \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\)
- Central atom: Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) in the anion.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\), sodium is the cation \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) with an oxidation number of \(+1\). The corresponding anion is the hypophosphite ion, \([\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2]^-\). By convention, hydrogen bonded to non-metals is assigned an oxidation state of \(+1\), and oxygen is assigned \(-2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in a polyatomic ion equals the charge of the ion:
\[\sum \text{Oxidation numbers} = \text{Net charge}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Let the oxidation number of phosphorus be \(x\). In the anion \([\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2]^-\):
\[2(+1) + x + 2(-2) = -1\]
\[2 + x - 4 = -1\]
\[x - 2 = -1\]
\[x = -1 + 2 = +1\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The oxidation state of the central phosphorus atom is \(+1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - Identification of non tetrahedral molecular geometry

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not tetrahedral in shape?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The molecular shape of a covalent chemical species is determined by the steric number of the central atom (number of bond pairs plus lone pairs) according to Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\): The central nitrogen atom has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs. The steric number is 4, giving \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybridisation and a tetrahedral shape.
- \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\): The central silicon atom has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs. The steric number is 4, giving \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybridisation and a tetrahedral shape.
- \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\): The central sulphur atom has 4 \(\sigma\)-bonds and 0 lone pairs. The steric number is 4, giving \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybridisation and a tetrahedral shape.
- \(\mathrm{SF}_4\): The central sulphur atom has 6 valence electrons, forms 4 single bonds with fluorine atoms, and retains one non-bonding lone pair (steric number = \(4 + 1 = 5\)). This corresponds to \(\mathrm{sp}^3\mathrm{d}\) hybridisation with a trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. Because the lone pair occupies an equatorial position to minimise repulsions, the molecular geometry is see-saw.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) has a see-saw geometry, it is not tetrahedral in shape.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Identification of peroxoacids of sulphur

questiontext.text: Which of the following are peroxoacids of sulphur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A peroxoacid contains at least one peroxy linkage (\(-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}-\)), wherein the oxygen atoms possess an oxidation state of \(-1\).

Step 2: Structural Analysis of Given Oxoacids
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) (peroxomonosulphuric acid, commonly known as Caro's acid): Contains one peroxy group directly bonded to the sulphur centre, represented structurally as \(\mathrm{HO}-\mathrm{SO}_2-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\).
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\) (peroxodisulphuric acid, commonly known as Marshall's acid): Contains two tetrahedral sulphur units connected by a central peroxy bridge, represented structurally as \(\mathrm{HO}-\mathrm{SO}_2-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{SO}_2-\mathrm{OH}\).
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_7\) (pyrosulphuric acid or oleum): Contains a normal ether-like oxygen bridge (\(-\mathrm{O}-\)) between two sulphur atoms without any peroxy linkage, represented structurally as \(\mathrm{HO}-\mathrm{SO}_2-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{SO}_2-\mathrm{OH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the peroxoacids of sulphur are \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Oxidation of non metals into two gaseous products

questiontext.text: Hot conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as moderately strong oxidising agent. It oxidises both metals and nonmetals. Which of the following element is oxidised by conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) into two gaseous products?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hot concentrated sulphuric acid undergoes thermal decomposition to furnish sulphur dioxide, water, and nascent oxygen:
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + [\mathrm{O}]\]
The nascent oxygen then oxidises metals or non-metals present in the reaction mixture.

Step 2: Examination of the Reactions with Each Element
- Copper (\(\mathrm{Cu}\)):
\[\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Produces only one gaseous product (\(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Zinc (\(\mathrm{Zn}\)):
\[\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Produces only one gaseous product (\(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}\)):
\[\mathrm{S} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow 3\mathrm{SO}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Produces only one gaseous product (\(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Carbon (\(\mathrm{C}\)):
\[\mathrm{C} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{SO}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Produces two distinct gaseous products: carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)) and sulphur dioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the element oxidised by concentrated sulphuric acid into two gaseous products is carbon (C).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Oxidation state shift during nitrogen trichloride synthesis

questiontext.text: A black compound of manganese reacts with a halogen acid to give greenish yellow gas. When excess of this gas reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) an unstable trihalide is formed. In this process the oxidation state of nitrogen changes from

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Reactants and Intermediates
The black manganese compound is manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO}_2\)). When heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)), it produces greenish-yellow chlorine gas:
\[\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2 + \mathrm{Cl}_2\uparrow + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 2: Reaction with Ammonia
When excess chlorine gas reacts with ammonia, the explosive, unstable trihalide nitrogen trichloride (\(\mathrm{NCl}_3\)) is formed:
\[\mathrm{NH}_3 + 3\mathrm{Cl}_2(\text{excess}) \rightarrow \mathrm{NCl}_3 + 3\mathrm{HCl}\]

Step 3: Determination of Oxidation States of Nitrogen
- In ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)): Hydrogen has an oxidation state of \(+1\).
\[x + 3(+1) = 0 \implies x = -3\]
- In nitrogen trichloride (\(\mathrm{NCl}_3\)): Chlorine has a higher Pauling electronegativity (3.16) than nitrogen (3.04), and therefore chlorine is assigned an oxidation state of \(-1\).
\[y + 3(-1) = 0 \implies y = +3\]
Thus, the oxidation state of nitrogen shifts from \(-3\) to \(+3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the oxidation state of nitrogen changes from -3 to +3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Ionisation enthalpy rationale for xenon compound synthesis

questiontext.text: In the preparation of compounds of Xe, Bartlett had taken \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\) as a base compound. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical and Conceptual Principle
In 1962, Neil Bartlett prepared the ionic compound dioxygenyl hexafluoroplatinate(V), \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\left[\mathrm{PtF}_6\right]^-\), by reacting molecular oxygen with the powerful oxidising agent platinum hexafluoride (\(\mathrm{PtF}_6\)).

Step 2: Comparison of Ionisation Enthalpies
Bartlett noted that the first ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen to produce the dioxygenyl cation is \(1175\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\), which is nearly identical to the first ionisation enthalpy of xenon, \(1170\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Reasoning and Chemical Synthesis
Because xenon requires almost the same energy to lose an electron as molecular oxygen does, Bartlett concluded that platinum hexafluoride should also be capable of oxidising xenon. Mixing xenon with \(\mathrm{PtF}_6\) resulted in the synthesis of the first noble gas compound, \(\mathrm{Xe}^+\left[\mathrm{PtF}_6\right]^-\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Bartlett used \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\) as a base compound because both \(\mathrm{O}_2\) and Xe have almost the same ionisation enthalpy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Structural state of phosphorus pentachloride in crystal

questiontext.text: In solid state \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is a

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phosphorus pentachloride exists as discrete, trigonal bipyramidal covalent molecules in the vapour and liquid phases. In the crystalline solid state, it undergoes ionisation to form a stable ionic lattice.

Step 2: Solid-State Ionisation
To relieve steric crowding and maximise lattice energy, two neutral \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) molecules autoionise into a pair of complex ions:
\[2\mathrm{PCl}_5(\text{s}) \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+ \left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\]

Step 3: Geometry and Coordination of Constituent Ions
- The cation \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\) has 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs on phosphorus, giving \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybridisation and a tetrahedral geometry.
- The anion \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\) has 6 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs on phosphorus, giving \(\mathrm{sp}^3\mathrm{d}^2\) hybridisation and an octahedral geometry.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, in the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is an ionic solid with \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_{4}\right]^{+}\) tetrahedral and \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_{6}\right]^{-}\) octahedra.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Ranking oxidizing strength from standard reduction potentials

questiontext.text:
Reduction potentials of some ions are given below. Arrange them in decreasing order of oxidising power.

Ion\(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{IO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\)
Reduction potential \(E^\circ/\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.19\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.65\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potentials (\(E^\circ\)) of the perhalate ions:
- \(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\): \(E^\circ = 1.19\,\mathrm{V}\)
- \(\mathrm{IO}_4^-\): \(E^\circ = 1.65\,\mathrm{V}\)
- \(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\): \(E^\circ = 1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard reduction potential reflects the thermodynamic tendency of a chemical species to accept electrons and undergo reduction. A more positive reduction potential indicates greater ease of reduction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Because an oxidising agent oxidises other substances by accepting electrons and being reduced itself, its oxidising power is directly proportional to its standard reduction potential:
\[\text{Oxidising power} \propto E^\circ_{\text{red}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Arranging the ions in decreasing order of their standard reduction potentials:
\[1.74\,\mathrm{V} (\mathrm{BrO}_4^-) > 1.65\,\mathrm{V} (\mathrm{IO}_4^-) > 1.19\,\mathrm{V} (\mathrm{ClO}_4^-)\]
Consequently, the oxidising power decreases in the sequence:
\[\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct decreasing order of oxidising power is \(\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Identification of an isoelectronic polyatomic pair

questiontext.text: Which of the following is isoelectronic pair?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Two chemical species are classified as an isoelectronic pair if they possess the identical total number of electrons.

Step 2: Total Electron Count Determination
Calculate the total electron count for each species by summing the atomic numbers of constituent atoms and adjusting for ionic charges:
- Pair with \(\mathrm{ICl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\):
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{ICl}_2 = 53 + 2(17) = 87\)
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{ClO}_2 = 17 + 2(8) = 33\) (unequal)
- Pair with \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+\):
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^- = 35 + 2(8) + 1 = 35 + 16 + 1 = 52\)
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+ = 35 + 2(9) - 1 = 35 + 18 - 1 = 52\)
Both species contain 52 electrons, confirming they are isoelectronic.
- Pair with \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}\):
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{ClO}_2 = 17 + 2(8) = 33\)
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{BrF} = 35 + 9 = 44\) (unequal)
- Pair with \(\mathrm{CN}^-\) and \(\mathrm{O}_3\):
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{CN}^- = 6 + 7 + 1 = 14\)
Total electrons in \(\mathrm{O}_3 = 3(8) = 24\) (unequal)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the isoelectronic pair is \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-,\, \mathrm{BrF}_2^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Oxidation state shifts of chlorine in hot alkali

questiontext.text: If chlorine gas is passed through hot \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, two changes are observed in the oxidation number of chlorine during the reaction. These are ______ and ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When chlorine gas reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide, it undergoes a disproportionation reaction, simultaneously undergoing self-oxidation and self-reduction.

Step 2: Chemical Reaction with Hot Concentrated Alkali
In hot and concentrated alkaline solution, chlorine disproportionates to give sodium chloride, sodium chlorate, and water:
\[3\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 6\mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 5\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{NaClO}_3 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]

Step 3: Changes in Oxidation Number
- Initial reactant state: In elemental chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)), the oxidation number of chlorine is \(0\).
- Reduction: In sodium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaCl}\)), sodium is \(+1\), so chlorine has an oxidation number of \(-1\). This represents a change from \(0\) to \(-1\).
- Oxidation: In sodium chlorate (\(\mathrm{NaClO}_3\)), sodium is \(+1\) and oxygen is \(-2\). Let the oxidation number of chlorine be \(x\):
\[+1 + x + 3(-2) = 0 \implies x - 5 = 0 \implies x = +5\]
This represents a change from \(0\) to \(+5\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the two changes observed in the oxidation number of chlorine during the reaction are 0 to +5 and 0 to -1.
